suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the incoming request context (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`) in Create (lines 50-57), and the same pattern is used in Delete (108-114), Update (134-141) and DeleteCollection (161-167). WHY: The apiserver request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and the goroutine performs the legacy write after Create/Update/Delete returns — so in production the legacy 'safe measure' write races request-context cancellation and will commonly fail with context.Canceled. The failure is silent because, unlike the previous synchronous code, the goroutines never log the legacy error, they only record a metric. Mode 3 can therefore appear healthy while legacy storage steadily drifts out of sync. HOW: Detach the goroutine context from request cancellation, e.g. `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), time.Second*10, ...)` (this repo already uses context.WithoutCancel in pkg/services/authn/authnimpl/sync), and log the legacy write error inside the goroutine.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Update now passes the raw `objInfo` to the asynchronous `d.Legacy.Update` (line 139); the previous implementation fetched `old` from unified storage, computed `updated := objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)`, and passed `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: ...}` to legacy so both stores wrote the identical object (the wrapper pattern still exists in dualwriter.go:128 and is used by mode 1 and mode 2). WHY: Legacy storage now recomputes `UpdatedObject` against its own old object, asynchronously and possibly after the request ended — if legacy state has diverged from unified (e.g. objects created before mode 3, or earlier async writes dropped by the request-context cancellation), the object persisted to legacy differs from the one persisted to unified, defeating mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy as a consistent fallback. It also invokes the caller's UpdatedObjectInfo a second time after Storage.Update already consumed it, which is not guaranteed to be safe/idempotent for apiserver-provided implementations. HOW: Before spawning the goroutine, compute the updated object from the unified-store result and pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` to Legacy.Update, mirroring dualwriter_mode2.go:298.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` (also `startStorage` is passed as the start time) even though legacy storage was never invoked; the identical mistake exists in Update at line 129. WHY: Storage create/update failures are recorded into the `grafana_dual_writer_legacy_duration_seconds` histogram (metrics.go:54-57) while the storage histogram never sees the error, so alerting/dashboards built on these metrics misattribute unified-storage outages to legacy and hide real storage error rates. suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete success path passes the individual resource name as a Prometheus metric label instead of the resource kind, exposing object names on the /metrics endpoint.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Line 106 passes the per-object `name` (the deleted resource's name) as the third argument to recordStorageDuration, whose signature (metrics.go:59) treats it as the metric's name/kind label. Pass `options.Kind` instead of `name`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Legacy writes are now fire-and-forget goroutines that reuse the request context, so they are canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns and the dual-write contract ('writes to LegacyStorage and Storage') is silently broken.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The legacy write moved from synchronous to a fire-and-forget goroutine, but it still derives its context from the request ctx. The request context is canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection will run with a canceled context and nearly always fail — callers that previously could rely on the legacy write being complete on return (legacy API readers, sync/migration logic) lose that guarantee with no error surfaced. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (plus the timeout) inside the goroutine, and log the error, since it is now invisible to the caller. Apply the same fix in Delete (:108-114), Update (:134-141), and DeleteCollection (:161-167).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete now returns early on any unified-storage error including NotFound, removing the fallback that used to still delete the object from legacy storage, so legacy-only objects become undeletable orphans in mode 3.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The old Delete tolerated a NotFound from unified storage and still deleted from LegacyStorage; the new early return on any error drops that fallback. Objects that exist only in legacy storage (anything created before the unified store took over) can no longer be deleted in mode 3 — the caller gets NotFound and the legacy copy is orphaned. Restore the IsNotFound fall-through (and tolerate NotFound from the legacy delete as before).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Update no longer pins the legacy write to the object unified storage produced (updateWrapper removed), so the legacy copy is recomputed independently and can diverge from the unified copy, and UpdatedObject is now invoked twice.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Previously the legacy update was forced (via updateWrapper) to persist the exact object returned by unified storage, keeping the two stores identical and calling UpdatedObject only once. Now the raw objInfo is handed to both stores, so legacy recomputes the object against its own old state — resourceVersion/UID can diverge between stores, and UpdatedObject runs twice, which breaks UpdatedObjectInfo implementations that are not idempotent. Wrap res in updateWrapper for the legacy call (as the old code did) while keeping the async write.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: None of the Mode3 tests await or assert the async legacy writes, so deleting the legacy half of the dual-writer — the defining behavior of Mode 3 — leaves every test green.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Mode 3's contract is 'write to LegacyStorage and Storage, read from Storage', but the tests only ever verify the storage half. The legacy write runs in a background goroutine (dualwriter_mode3.go:50-57, 108-114, 134-141, 161-167) that the tests never synchronize with, and no test calls m.AssertExpectations(t) or m.AssertCalled(t, "Create", ...) on the legacy mock. The legacy expectation registered in setupLegacyFn (lines 30-32) is therefore vacuous — it passes whether Legacy.Create is invoked or not. If someone removed the legacy writes from DualWriterMode3 entirely, the whole test file would still pass. Fix: make the dual writer expose a way to flush/await the legacy goroutine (or inject a synchronous executor in tests), and assert on the legacy mock, e.g. wait for the call then m.AssertCalled(t, "Create", mock.Anything, exampleObj, mock.Anything, mock.Anything), plus a negative case asserting legacy errors are not surfaced.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection register no legacy mock expectations at all, so the legacy deletion path of Mode 3 is completely unverified.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The Delete and DeleteCollection tests never set up or assert the legacy store, even though DualWriterMode3.Delete/DeleteCollection delete from Legacy in a goroutine after the storage delete succeeds. The shared mock `m` masks this: the goroutine's Legacy.Delete call matches the storage expectation (same method name and signature), so nothing observes whether the legacy delete ran, failed, or was skipped. A regression that drops the legacy delete (or lets it error) passes these tests. Add a legacy expectation and synchronize on the goroutine before asserting, e.g. require.Eventually on m.Calls followed by m.AssertCalled(t, "Delete", mock.Anything, tt.input, mock.Anything, mock.Anything), and a case where legacy delete fails while storage succeeds, asserting the method still returns the storage result.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The case named 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' injects the failure through setupLegacyFn and only passes because the legacy and storage mocks share one *mock.Mock, so it cannot tell which store failed.
suggestions.suggestionContent: This test intends to verify that a unified-store create failure propagates, but the failing expectation is registered through setupLegacyFn and relies on `m` being shared between legacyStoreMock and storageMock — the expectation matches a call from either store. Give the two mocks separate *mock.Mock instances (or distinct expectation matchers), register the failure on the storage mock, and add the inverse case (legacy fails, storage succeeds) asserting err == nil to pin down that legacy errors are ignored in Mode 3.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Async legacy writes derive from the request context, so they are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns and the two stores silently diverge.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The fire-and-forget goroutine wraps the incoming request ctx with context.WithTimeoutCause. This DualWriter is invoked by the apiserver handler chain, so ctx is the HTTP request context, which Go cancels when ServeHTTP returns — i.e., right after Create returns. The legacy write is therefore almost always aborted with context.Canceled before or during the legacy store call; the 10s timeout never takes effect. Mode 3's core invariant ('writes go to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage') is silently broken: unified storage gets the object, legacy does not, and the error is only recorded to metrics (never logged), so the stores diverge with no signal. The same pattern exists in Delete (lines 108-114), Update (134-141) and DeleteCollection (161-167). Fix: detach from the request context before applying the timeout, e.g. `ctx = context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (Go 1.21+) inside or before the goroutine, and log legacy write failures.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Update passes the raw objInfo to the async legacy update, so legacy recomputes a potentially different object than the one written to unified storage, and concurrent updates can be applied to legacy out of order.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The removed code wrapped the object produced by the storage update in updateWrapper so that BOTH stores persisted the exact same object. Now the same objInfo is handed to d.Legacy.Update in the goroutine, so the legacy store calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld) a second time against its own old object — any divergence between the stores' old objects (guaranteed once finding 1 drops a legacy write) produces a different object in legacy than in unified storage, breaking the dual-write same-object invariant. In addition, because the legacy write is async with no ordering, two concurrent updates to the same name can be applied to legacy in the opposite order from storage (A-storage, B-storage, B-legacy, A-legacy), leaving legacy permanently stale while reads come from storage. Restore the pin-the-result approach: compute the updated object from the storage result and pass an updateWrapper-style UpdatedObjectInfo to the legacy call, and consider serializing legacy writes per object (or making them synchronous) to preserve ordering.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The async legacy Create mutates the caller's obj concurrently with the caller serializing the returned object, risking a data race and legacy values leaking into the response.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The goroutine passes the caller's `obj` to d.Legacy.Create while the caller proceeds to serialize `created`. Kubernetes storage convention mutates the input object in place (PrepareForCreate stamps UID, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp) and stores commonly return the same pointer, so `created` and `obj` are typically the same object. The legacy create's in-place mutations then race with response serialization and can overwrite the unified-store UID/RV in the response body. Pre-PR the legacy call was synchronous before return, so there was no concurrency; this PR introduces the race. Pass a DeepCopyObject() of obj (or of created) to the legacy call, or perform the legacy write synchronously before returning.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Create:45 and Update:129 record legacy duration when the storage call fails, misattributing storage errors to the legacy latency metric.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In Mode3 Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), the legacy duration metric is recorded on the storage-failure path. recordLegacyDuration should reflect the legacy call's own latency/outcome; when the Storage call fails and returns early, the legacy duration must not be recorded, otherwise storage errors pollute the legacy latency metric.

suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Removing the whole-function cacheMu lock lets two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the SAME NamespacedResource build in parallel, because the only callers reach it via a check-then-act with no per-key synchronization: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:292-298, which even carries a TODO admitting the missing per-key blocking) is called concurrently from Search (search.go:148 and the federated loop at :160, i.e. parallel gRPC requests) and from the watch-event goroutine handleEvent (search.go:237). WHY: for an unindexed namespace/resource (e.g. count <= InitMinCount, or a newly-created kind) two requests — or a search racing a write event — both see GetIndex==nil and both build: (a) when size > FileThreshold both call bleve.New(dir, mapper) on the SAME on-disk directory (bleve.go:97-98), so one build fails with 'cannot create new index, path exists' and the search request errors out, or both interleave creation and corrupt the scorch/bolt files; (b) both goroutines then race to b.cache[key] = idx (bleve.go:137-139), last-writer-wins, and the losing fully-built index is dropped without Close (no Close anywhere in the overwrite path), leaking file handles/memory. Previously the function-wide lock serialized these duplicates; now they execute concurrently. The previous order (watch first, then build) ensured such events were observed and re-applied. Unless initWatcher replays from a resource version at or before the build snapshot, this loses events; either restore the previous ordering or have the watcher start from the RV captured at the start of search.init.

WHY: DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext (lines 57-60) reads a null attribute and falls back to "na", so every access token issued via the client credentials grant — one of the most common grants, and the one the new unit test uses as its showcase ("trltcc:1234") — is encoded with grant type "na" instead of "cc"; PermissionGrantType's delegation to clientCredentialsGrant.process (PermissionGrantType.java:122) inherits the same gap. HOW: add clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, context.getGrantType()) in ClientCredentialsGrantType.process before tokenManager.responseBuilder(...) is invoked (e.g. right after line 122 where clientSessionCtx is attached).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Javadoc advertises a "3-letters shortcut" but every implementation returns 2 letters and the decoder hard-codes exactly 2 chars for the grant shortcut.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Comment claims the grant-type shortcut "starts at character 4th char" but the encoder places it at characters 5-6, so the matcher (following the comment) checks the wrong two characters.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says the grant-type shortcut "starts at character 4th char", but per DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider the 6-char context is 2 chars sessionType + 2 chars tokenType + 2 chars grantType, so the grant shortcut starts at the 5th character (index 4). The matcher code follows the wrong comment and extracts substring(3, 5) — the last tokenType char plus the first grantType char — so these new assertions never verify the actual grant shortcut. Fix the comment to "starts at character 5th char" and use substring(4, 6) (and negate the equals so a match doesn't return false).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The rawTokenId null-check in the constructor accidentally re-checks grantType, so the non-null invariant on rawTokenId is never enforced.

A null rawTokenId is therefore silently accepted, and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` (line 117) would concatenate it into a token ID literally ending in `:null` instead of failing fast. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted equality logic and an off-by-one substring, so the grant-type assertion it adds never actually verifies the grant type.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In `matchesSafely`: (1) the grant shortcut occupies chars 4-5 of the 6-char context prefix (sessionType 0-1, tokenType 2-3, grant 4-5 — as the code's own comment states), so it must be `items[0].substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)` which spans the tokenType's last char and the grant's first char; (2) the condition is inverted — it returns `false` (no match) when the extracted shortcut EQUALS the expected one. Because of (1), the equality never holds for a correct token, so the guard is dead and the matcher degenerates to a `prefix:UUID` shape check — the grant assertions this PR added to expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/etc. silently verify nothing, and fixing only the offset would flip every one of those assertions to failing. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The lazy map-refresh paths insert runtime-discovered grants without the duplicate-shortcut validation that postInit enforces, so a colliding shortcut silently corrupts the shortcut<->grant bijection.
suggestions.suggestionContent: postInit validates that grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts stay the same size (no two grants share an ID or shortcut). The lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType (lines 109-116) and getGrantTypeByShortcut (lines 123-134) skips that validation: a grant provider deployed at runtime whose shortcut collides with an existing grant's shortcut would overwrite grantsByShortcuts (so tokens of the other grant decode as this one) while grantsToShortcuts keeps both entries, silently breaking the 1:1 invariant. The concurrent interleaving itself is safe (ConcurrentHashMap, both racing threads compute the same value), but consider detecting an existing different mapping on the lazy path, e.g. with putIfAbsent plus an equality check.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Context captures grantType from formParams only in the constructor, but the retained setFormParams mutator does not refresh it, so grantType can go stale relative to the current form params.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The constructor now derives `grantType` from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)` (line 102), and OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse later stamps `context.getGrantType()` into the client session context (from where it is encoded into the token ID). However `setFormParams(MultivaluedHashMap)` (line 105) is still part of the class and does not update grantType, so any flow that replaces the form params after constructing the Context would leave getGrantType() returning the value from the original params — a stale-state inconsistency. Either update grantType inside setFormParams as well, or derive it lazily in getGrantType() from the current formParams.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Inverted condition and off-by-one substring make the grant-shortcut matcher always pass, so the updated event assertions cannot detect a broken grant-type encoding.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The isAccessTokenId matcher never actually verifies the grant shortcut, so all four updated event expectations (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) would still pass if the grant-type encoding in the token ID were broken. Two defects combine here: (1) wrong substring bounds — the encoded 6-char prefix is sessionType(chars 0-1) + tokenType(chars 2-3) + grantType(chars 4-5) per DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider, so the grant shortcut is substring(4, 6), but the matcher extracts substring(3, 5) (2nd char of tokenType + 1st char of grant, e.g. "onrtac" → "ta"); (2) inverted condition — `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` rejects when the extracted string MATCHES the expected shortcut, so even with correct bounds it would fail on correct tokens; the negation `!` is missing. suggestions.label: bug

The fixture in before() never calls postInit, so factory.sessionFactory is null; looking up the unregistered "ac" shortcut enters the 'refresh maps' fallback in getGrantTypeByShortcut and throws a NullPointerException at sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...) — not the intended IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type"). suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: isAccessTokenId reads the grant shortcut at the wrong offset (substring(3,5) instead of (4,6)) and with inverted equality, so the grant-type assertion added by this PR is silently vacuous.

Because index 3 is always 't' or 'n', the equals branch effectively never fires and the matcher passes any grant shortcut as long as the tail is a UUID — tests expecting e.g. the "ac" shortcut would also accept "rt"/"dg" tokens. Fix: `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Unhandled exceptions from get_user_info (raise_for_status/network/JSON) turn transient GitHub failures into 500s instead of the error page.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called outside any try/except, but its implementation (src/sentry/identity/github/provider.py:7-17) calls `resp.raise_for_status()` and `resp.json()`, so any GitHub API error (5xx, rate limit), network failure (ConnectionError/Timeout), or non-JSON body raises an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of the graceful github-integration-failed page this view uses everywhere else (the token-exchange parsing directly above wraps failures in try/except for exactly this reason). Fix: wrap the call, e.g. `try: authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) except Exception: return error(request, self.active_organization)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Direct metadata["sender"]["login"] indexing crashes with KeyError for integrations whose metadata lacks a sender (which the codebase itself acknowledges can happen).
suggestions.suggestionContent: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` raises KeyError when the Integration's metadata has no `sender` key, which is a real state: build_integration (lines 376-377) only stores sender when the pipeline state contains it, the sibling endpoint src/sentry/integrations/github/installation.py:44 explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and test_basic_flow asserts metadata with no sender for pipeline-created integrations. When such an Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration (e.g. the installation.created webhook never ran and the org link was later removed), any install attempt with that installation_id crashes with a 500 instead of failing closed. Fix: use a guarded lookup and treat absence as a mismatch, e.g. `sender_login = integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and `if not sender_login or pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != sender_login: return error(...)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The sender check is skipped entirely when the Integration row doesn't exist yet (webhook lag), leaving an installation-hijack race window the PR claims to close.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new authenticated-user-vs-installer validation only executes when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds; in the `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch (line 482) the pipeline advances to completion with `github_authenticated_user` never compared to anyone. GitHub redirects the browser to the setup URL synchronously right after the app is installed, while the installation.created webhook that creates the Integration row (webhook.py:201-210) is asynchronous and can be delayed, backlogged, or unconfigured — in that window the record does not exist and the check is silently skipped. An attacker who knows or guesses a victim's fresh installation_id (GitHub installation ids are sequential integers visible in redirect URLs) can race the webhook and attach the victim's installation to their own Sentry organization, which is exactly the attack this PR is meant to block; the legitimate user is then locked out with "installed on another Sentry organization". Fix: in the DoesNotExist path, verify ownership before advancing — e.g. fetch the installation via get_installation_info(installation_id) and require the GitHub API response's account/permissions to be consistent with the authenticated user, or fail closed and ask the user to retry once the webhook has landed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Applying _() to the error_short variable instead of to the string literals makes these user-facing error messages unextractable and permanently English-only, a regression from the pre-PR code.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `_(error_short)` wraps a variable, so the short error messages are never extracted for translation. The values passed — the default "Invalid installation request." (line 132), "GitHub installation pending deletion." (line 471), and "Github installed on another Sentry organization." (line 488) — are plain string literals at the call sites, and gettext extraction (makemessages) only collects *literal* arguments to `_()`. Before this PR these exact strings were literals wrapped directly in `_()` at the render site and were extractable; after this refactor they will always render in English, unlike the neighbouring `error_long` constants (`ERR_INTEGRATION_*`) which are module-level `_()` literals and remain translatable. Fix by wrapping the literals at their definition/call sites, e.g. `error_short=_("GitHub installation pending deletion.")` and `error_short=_("Invalid installation request.")` as the default, and pass `error_short` through unwrapped in the payload (the payload is serialized with `json.dumps` in the template, so a lazy proxy is acceptable there as it is for `error`).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Network/API failures in the OAuth token exchange and user-info lookup are outside the try/except and surface as unhandled 500s instead of the intended error page.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The failure handling in OAuthLoginView.dispatch is incomplete: `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) is executed BEFORE the try/except, so a connection error/timeout to GitHub raises an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of the graceful github-integration-failed page this PR adds. Likewise `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) can raise ApiError if the token is rejected by the /user endpoint, and that also escapes. The PR clearly intends to degrade gracefully (it returns error() when access_token is missing from the payload), so wrap the safe_urlopen and get_user_info calls in try/except and fall through to `return error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Hard metadata["sender"]["login"] indexing raises KeyError for Integration rows whose metadata predates or lacks the sender field.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` uses hard key lookups against an Integration row fetched only by external_id. Any pre-existing github Integration row (created before this change shipped) — or one created by a path that never recorded the webhook sender — will have no "sender" key in metadata, so the re-install/link flow this check protects will raise KeyError and 500 rather than showing the failure page. Use a defensive lookup such as `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a mismatch (or otherwise handle it) instead of raising.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The OAuth state parameter is compared to the pipeline signature with a non-constant-time != instead of hmac.compare_digest.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The OAuth `state` value is an anti-CSRF token binding GitHub's callback to this pipeline session, and it is verified with a plain `!=` string comparison (line 412), which short-circuits on the first differing byte. For secret/session tokens the standard is a constant-time comparison (e.g. `hmac.compare_digest(request.GET.get("state", ""), pipeline.signature)`), matching how Django compares CSRF tokens. Real-world exploitability over the network is low, but the hardening is one line and removes any timing side channel on the value that gates the installation flow.

suggestions.suggestionContent: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` takes a `value: int` parameter but never uses it — the occurrence is built only from `handler`, `group_key`, and `new_status`. As a result, the tests that call it cannot detect the value being propagated incorrectly: `test_results_on_change` evaluates a packet with `{"val1": 100}` but builds the expected occurrence with value `6`, `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` uses packet value `8` vs expected `6`, and `test_state_results_multi_group` gives `group_2` the value `10` but builds `occurrence_2` with `6` — and they all still pass. Either incorporate `value` into the built occurrence (e.g., into `evidence_data`) so the expectation actually depends on it, or fix the call sites to pass the packet's real value and drop the pretense that value is verified.
